subject: Arabic

source.title: Junior School Curriculum Design — Arabic Grade 9 (First published 2023, Revised 2024)
source.notes: Unlike Grade 8 Arabic (where README.md's currency-check notes record that only a 2022-draft/JSS-branded mirror could be found, no 2024-dated copy), a genuinely current Grade 9 copy WAS found on the first search: easylearn.co.ke's 'FINAL-ARABIC-GRADE-9-CURRICULUM-DESIGN.pdf'. WebFetch reported the extracted text was corrupted PDF-object-stream binary (a known WebFetch limitation for this file type) but confirmed it had saved the file locally; Claude's Read tool then parsed the saved PDF natively and returned clean text for all 75 pages. Cover page reads 'JUNIOR SCHOOL CURRICULUM DESIGN / ARABIC / GRADE 9', copyright page confirms 'First published 2023 / Revised 2024', ISBN 978-9914-43-447-7, Foreword signed by the current CS Hon. Ezekiel Ombaki Machogu, CBS — the same currency-confirmation pattern used successfully for the Grade 8 Arabic re-sourcing pass. Full document body (pages 1-63, all 9 themes across all 3 strands, both assessment rubrics per strand, Appendix 1 CSL guidelines, Appendix 2 resources table) was read directly and transcribed verbatim below, not summarized by an intermediate model.

essenceNote: As part of the international community, Kenyan learners will have the opportunity to learn foreign languages in addition to the national, official, and indigenous languages. These foreign languages include Arabic, French, German, and Mandarin. The curriculum aims for learners to acquire basic proficiency in the four language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. This will give the learner an opportunity to develop language competencies in an experiential, innovative, and flexible ways. Foreign language learning at this level is guided by social-constructivist and environmental theories. Learning these languages will promote international awareness and appreciation of one's own and others' cultures. By transitioning to Senior School, the learner will have achieved basic proficiency equivalent to A1/YCT2 level. (Verbatim, identical wording pattern to French/German/Mandarin Grade 9's essence statements.)

generalLearningOutcomes.scope: By the end of Middle School (i.e. across the Junior School cycle, not Grade 9 alone)
generalLearningOutcomes.notes: Verbatim from the source document's 'GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR ARABIC LANGUAGE' section (p.xi). Recorded for reference; not used directly to generate Grade-9-specific quiz content since these outcomes span the full cycle.
outcomes: listen and respond appropriately to relevant information in the Arabic language,
read a wide variety of texts fluently and accurately for lifelong learning,
write texts legibly, coherently, and creatively in the Arabic language,
express themselves fluently and confidently in varied contexts,
appreciate the role of the Arabic language as a means of embracing creativity and international relevance,
enjoy communicating in the Arabic language,
appreciate cultural awareness and exposure to the Arabic language.

strands.name: 1.0 Listening and Speaking
strands.summaryTableNote: The source's 'SUMMARY OF STRANDS AND SUB-STRANDS' table (p.xii) aggregates by sub-strand NAME rather than listing all 9 theme-based entries individually, and — unlike Grade 8's version of this same table, which was internally self-consistent — this Grade 9 table appears to contain a genuine transcription artifact: it lists 'Active Speaking (2)' as a row distinct from 'Active Listening (2)', but no sub-strand anywhere in the document body (1.1-1.9) is actually named 'Active Speaking' — only 'Active Listening' (at 1.3 and 1.8, which would sum to 4 lessons, not the 2 shown against either row). The per-theme tables in the document body (used as the ground truth for the subStrands array below) are unambiguous and internally consistent themselves: 3x Interactive Speaking (1.1, 1.5, 1.9), 2x Listening for Information (1.2, 1.7), 2x Active Listening (1.3, 1.8), 2x Oral Expression (1.4, 1.6) = 9 sub-strands, 18 lessons total, matching the strand's own stated total.

subStrands.name: Interactive Speaking
specificLearningOutcomes: identify basic greetings in formal contexts
apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication
appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication
keyInquiryQuestions: Why should we use polite language when interacting with others?
learningExperiences: listen to a conversation on greetings in formal situations
pick out words and phrases used to express greetings in formal contexts e.g. (assalamu alaykum, sabahal khayr, masala khayr, maa ismuka?, keyfa haaluka?, anaa masruurun biliqaika, shukran)

work jointly to role-play formal greetings in formal settings using non-verbal cues
practise using polite language in a conversation using words (i.e. May I …, can I borrow your pen please?, "Sorry", "Excuse me please?")
linkedLearningAreas: English — similar concepts of polite language
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric row 'Ability to display a willingness to participate in oral interactions' confirms active initiation/engagement in oral interaction (not just correct recall of greeting phrases) is part of the tested competency for this strand.

subStrands.name: Interactive Speaking

strands.assessmentSignal: Suggested Assessment Rubric for this strand (p.19-20) scores five indicators: (1) use of targeted vocabulary/expressions to probe and engage in oral interactions, (2) correct spoken-language patterns (pronunciation, intonation, rhythm, pacing), (3) responding to questions/prompts to show comprehension and engagement, (4) use of gestures and facial expressions (including sensitivity to cultural diversity in non-verbal cues at the top band), (5) willingness to initiate/participate in oral interactions. Confirms non-verbal-cue competence and willingness-to-engage are formally assessed dimensions, not just vocabulary recall.

strands.name: 2.0 Reading
strands.summaryTableNote: The source's summary table lists: Guided Reading: Reading Fluency (6), Guided Reading: Reading Aloud (2), Guided Reading: Reading Comprehension (2), Reading for information (6), Extensive Reading - Library skills (2). This aggregates several distinctly-named per-theme sub-strands under simplified umbrella labels — the per-theme tables in the document body (2.1-2.9, used as ground truth below) carry more specific names (e.g. '2.4 Reading Fluency: Pronunciation', '2.8 Reading for Information: Visuals', '2.5/2.6 Reading for Information') than the summary table's collapsed categories.

strands.assessmentSignal: Suggested Assessment Rubric for this strand (p.38-39) scores three indicators: (1) accurate pronunciation of words in context, (2) fluency (smoothness, pace, pauses, intonation) — top band explicitly requires auto-correcting own errors on unfamiliar-topic texts, (3) reading comprehension via ability to interpret and correctly answer questions with adequate/extensive vocabulary in responses.

strands.name: 3.0 Writing
strands.summaryTableNote: The source's summary table lists: Guided Writing: Paragraph Writing (2), Guided Writing: Handwriting (4), Guided Writing (6), Guided Writing: Imaginative Composition (2), Guided Writing: Summary Writing (2), Guided Writing: Poetry (2) — total 18. The generic 'Guided Writing (6)' row aggregates 3.3, 3.4, and 3.8, which the per-theme tables in the document body (used as ground truth below) name more specifically by their actual focus (vocabulary/simple sentences for 3.3, diary keeping for 3.4, key ideas/imaginative composition for 3.8).

strands.assessmentSignal: Suggested Assessment Rubric for this strand (p.57-58) scores three indicators: (1) writing clear, readable, neatly-spaced text (top band explicitly compares to a 'typed Microsoft Office Word document'), (2) organisation — logical/coherent sequence with clear beginning-middle-end and smooth transitions, (3) vocabulary variety and accuracy relative to topic. Confirms neatness/legibility and paragraph-level coherence are formally scored, not just correct spelling.

subStrands.name: Showcasing of skills and concepts (Exhibition)
subStrands.notes: Not one of the 27 theme-based sub-strands above — a standalone allocation (6 lessons; total document lesson count is 18+18+18+6=60, matching the source's own 'Total Number of Lessons: 60') tied to the Community Service Learning (CSL) project described in Appendix 1 (pp.59-60): a six-milestone whole-school group project (Problem Identification, Designing a solution, Planning, Implementation, Showcasing/Exhibition and Report Writing, Reflection) staggered across the three terms, assessed formatively against skills-applied, core-competencies-developed, and values-nurtured — not against any specific Arabic-language content outcome. No specific learning outcomes or key inquiry questions are attached to it in the source. Same structural role as the identically-named allocation in Grade 8 Arabic.

notes: Same 9 real-world themes (Greetings and Introduction, Family, My Surrounding, Time, Fun and Enjoyment, Food and Drinks, My Body, Weather and Environment, Getting Around) repeat identically across all 3 strands, exactly mirroring French/German/Mandarin Grade 9's structure — 27 distinct theme x strand sub-strands (1.1-1.9, 2.1-2.9, 3.1-3.9), each 2 sessions, matching this project's standing 'never merge sub-strands' rule (27 skills, not 9). Cross-checked against the 27 shipped skill files in web/src/skills/arabic/ (greetingsSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, familySpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, surroundingSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, timeSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, funSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, foodSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, bodySpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, weatherSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts, directionsSpeaking/Reading/Writing.ts) — the file-naming pattern (theme x {Speaking,Reading,Writing}) maps one-to-one onto all 27 sub-strands named above with no gaps: surrounding=My Surrounding, directions=Getting Around, food=Food and Drinks, body=My Body, weather=Weather and Environment, fun=Fun and Enjoyment. Spot-checked greetingsSpeaking.ts (branches on formal-greeting vocabulary e.g. assalamu alaykum/sabahal khayr/keyfa haaluka — matches sub-strand 1.1's learning-experiences vocabulary list verbatim), greetingsReading.ts (dialogue-comprehension using the same greeting vocabulary — matches 2.1's reading-fluency-on-greetings focus), and greetingsWriting.ts (fill-in-the-blank and sentence-ordering using the same phrases — matches 3.1's guided paragraph-writing/sequencing focus); all three correctly implement their sub-strand's actual modality rather than being copy-pasted repeats of each other. The 'Showcasing of skills and concepts (Exhibition)' allocation (6 lessons) is intentionally NOT built as a quiz skill, consistent with how Grade 8 Arabic treats the same allocation, since it is a whole-school CSL project assessed formatively against process/competency criteria rather than any single Arabic-language content outcome.
